L189: The rest of our derivation proceeds in two steps. First, we characterize the stochastic dynamics of $\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\leftarrow}$ under the target measure ${\mathbb{Q}}$. Second, by invoking the weak uniqueness of solutions to stochastic differential equations (cite132†Øksendal, 2003 , Lemma 5.3.1), we construct a controllable diffusion process under the base path measure ${\mathbb{P}}$ whose terminal distribution coincides with the target tilted distribution $q_{0}$.
L190: #### Dynamics under the target path measure
L191: 
L192: Girsanov’s theorem (cite132†Øksendal, 2003 , Theorem 8.6.8) establishes a fundamental correspondence between a drift shift in the driving Brownian motion and the dynamics of the associated Radon-Nikodym derivative process. Accordingly, we first characterize the evolution of the time-dependent likelihood ratio $L_{t}$.
L193: ###### Proposition 3.1 (Doob’s $h$-function).
L194: 
L195: The Radon-Nikodym derivative process $L_{t}$, as defined in (cite133†3.8 ), admits the following representation:
L196: 
L197:  | $$L_{t}={\mathbb{E}}^{{\mathbb{P}}}\Big[\frac{\,\mathrm{d}{\mathbb{Q}}}{\,\mathrm{d}{\mathbb{P}}}\Big|{\mathcal{F}}_{t}\Big]=\frac{h^{*}(t,\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\leftarrow})}{{\mathbb{E}}^{{\mathbb{P}}}[w(\mathbf{X}_{T}^{\leftarrow})]},$$  |
L198: where $h^{*}:[0,T]\times{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}$, referred to as Doob’s $h$-function, is defined as the conditional expectation of the terminal weight:
L199: 
L200:  | $$h^{*}(t,\mathbf{x})\coloneq{\mathbb{E}}^{{\mathbb{P}}}[w(\mathbf{X}_{T}^{\leftarrow})\mid\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\leftarrow}=\mathbf{x}].$$  |  | (3.10)
L201: 
L202: Furthermore, the log-likelihood ratio satisfies the following SDE:
L203:  | $$\,\mathrm{d}(\log L_{t})=\nabla\log h^{*}(t,\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\leftarrow})^{\top}\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}_{t}-\|\nabla\log h^{*}(t,\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\leftarrow})\|_{2}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t.$$  |
L204: 
L205: The proof of Proposition cite134†3.1 is provided in Appendix cite33†B . With the dynamics of $\log L_{t}$ established, we derive the stochastic dynamics of $\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\leftarrow}$ under the target measure ${\mathbb{Q}}$ via Girsanov’s theorem (cite132†Øksendal, 2003 , Theorem 8.6.6).
L206: ###### Proposition 3.2.
L207: 
L208: Let the base process $\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\leftarrow}$ satisfy the SDE (cite95†2.4 ) under the path measure ${\mathbb{P}}$, and let ${\mathbb{Q}}$ be the target path measure defined by (cite135†3.9 ). Assume that the Novikov condition holds:
L209: 
L210:  | $${\mathbb{E}}^{{\mathbb{P}}}\Big[\exp\Big(\int_{0}^{T}\|\nabla\log h^{*}(s,\mathbf{X}_{s}^{\leftarrow})\|_{2}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}s\Big)\Big]<\infty.$$  |  | (3.11)
L211: 
L212: Define a process $(\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_{t})_{1\leq t\leq T}$ by
L213:  | $$\,\mathrm{d}\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_{t}=\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}_{t}-\sqrt{2}\nabla\log h^{*}(t,\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\leftarrow})\,\mathrm{d}t,$$  |  | (3.12)
L214: 
L215: where $\mathbf{B}_{t}$ is a Brownian motion under ${\mathbb{P}}$. Then $\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_{t}$ is a standard Brownian motion under ${\mathbb{Q}}$. Further, under the path measure ${\mathbb{Q}}$, the base process $\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\leftarrow}$ in (cite95†2.4 ) evolves according to:
L216:  | $$\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\leftarrow}=(\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\leftarrow}+2\nabla\log p_{T-t}(\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\leftarrow})+2\nabla\log h^{*}(t,\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\leftarrow}))\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_{t}.$$  |  | (3.13)
L217: 
L218: The proof is deferred to Appendix cite33†B . By the construction in (cite135†3.9 ), the law of $\mathbf{X}_{T}^{\leftarrow}$ under ${\mathbb{Q}}$ coincides with the target tilted distribution $q_{0}$.
L219: ###### Remark 3.3 (Novikov condition).
L220: 
L221: The condition in (cite136†3.11 ) ensures that the exponential local martingale defined by the drift shift is a true martingale (cite137†Karatzas and Shreve, 1998 , Corollary 5.13), which is sufficient for the Radon-Nikodym derivative to be well-defined and for Girsanov’s theorem to apply.
L222: #### Controllable diffusion process under the base measure
L223: 
L224: Although Proposition cite138†3.2 constructs stochastic dynamics driven by Brownian motion under ${\mathbb{Q}}$ that achieve the desired terminal distribution $q_{0}$, practical implementation necessitates an SDE driven by Brownian motion under the reference measure ${\mathbb{P}}$.
L225: To address this, we construct a surrogate process $\mathbf{Z}_{t}^{\leftarrow}$ on the base probability space $(\Omega,{\mathcal{F}},{\mathbb{F}},{\mathbb{P}})$ that adopts the drift derived for ${\mathbb{Q}}$:
L226:  | $$\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{Z}_{t}^{\leftarrow}=\Big(\mathbf{Z}_{t}^{\leftarrow}+2\underbrace{\nabla\log p_{T-t}(\mathbf{Z}_{t}^{\leftarrow})}_{\text{base score}}+2\underbrace{\nabla\log h^{*}(t,\mathbf{Z}_{t}^{\leftarrow})}_{\text{Doob's guidance}}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}_{t}.$$  |  | (3.14)
L227: Since the process $\mathbf{Z}_{t}^{\leftarrow}$ driven by the ${\mathbb{P}}$-Brownian motion (cite139†3.14 ) satisfies the same SDE as $\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\leftarrow}$ driven by the ${\mathbb{Q}}$-Brownian motion (cite140†3.13 ), the weak uniqueness property of SDE solutions guarantees (cite132†Øksendal, 2003 , Lemma 5.3.1) that the law of $\mathbf{Z}_{t}^{\leftarrow}$ under ${\mathbb{P}}$ is identical to the law of $\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\leftarrow}$ under ${\mathbb{Q}}$ for all $t\in[0,T]$.
L228: Thus, the law of $\mathbf{Z}_{T}^{\leftarrow}$ under ${\mathbb{P}}$ coincides the target tilted distribution $q_{0}$. For a detailed formal statement, see cite132†Øksendal (2003, Theorem 8.6.8) .
L229: ### 3.3  Doob’s matching with gradient penalty
L230: 
L231: Up to now, we have found a controllable diffusion process (cite139†3.14 ) that can generate samples from the target tilted distribution $q_{0}$. However, the Doob’s $h$-function defined as (cite141†3.10 ) is intractable. This subsection aims to estimate the Doob’s guidance $\nabla\log h_{t}^{*}$ in (cite139†3.14 ).
L232: 
L233: For every $t\in(0,T)$, the Doob’s $h$-function $h_{t}^{*}\coloneq h^{*}(t,\cdot)$ is the unique solution to the following optimization problem:
L234:  | $$\min_{h_{t}:{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}}{\mathbb{E}}^{{\mathbb{P}}}\big[\|h_{t}(\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\leftarrow})-h_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\leftarrow})\|_{2}^{2}\big]=\|h_{t}-h_{t}^{*}\|_{L^{2}(p_{T-t})}^{2}.$$  |  | (3.15)
L235: However, since this objective functional includes unknown function $h_{t}^{*}$, we cannot use this explicit Doob’s matching objective functional. Based on the property of the conditional expectation (cite141†3.10 ), we now propose an alternative objective functional, named implicit Doob’s matching:
L236:  | $\displaystyle{\mathcal{J}}_{t}(h_{t})$  | $\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}^{{\mathbb{P}}}\big[\|h_{t}(\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\leftarrow})-w(\mathbf{X}_{T}^{\leftarrow})\|_{2}^{2}\big]$  |  | (3.16)
L237:  |  | $\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{X}_{0}\sim p_{0}}{\mathbb{E}}_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}\sim{\mathcal{N}}({\mathbf{0}},\mathbf{I}_{d})}\big[\|h_{t}(\mu_{T-t}\mathbf{X}_{0}+\sigma_{T-t}{\bm{\varepsilon}})-w(\mathbf{X}_{0})\|_{2}^{2}\big],$  |
L238: where $w:{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\to{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}$ is the known weight function defined as (cite131†3.1 ).
L239: 
L240: The following proposition bridges the objective functionals of the explicit Doob’s matching (cite142†3.15 ) and the implicit Doob’s matching (cite143†3.16 ).
L241: ###### Proposition 3.4.
L242: 
L243: For every $t\in(0,T)$, the Doob’s $h$-function $h_{t}^{*}$ in (cite141†3.10 ) minimizes the implicit Doob’s matching loss (cite143†3.16 ). Further,
L244: 
L245:  | $${\mathcal{J}}_{t}(h_{t})={\mathbb{E}}^{{\mathbb{P}}}\big[\|h_{t}(\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\leftarrow})-h_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\leftarrow})\|_{2}^{2}\big]+V_{t}^{2},$$  |
L246: 
L247: where $V_{t}^{2}\coloneq{\mathbb{E}}^{{\mathbb{P}}}[\mathrm{Var}(w(\mathbf{X}_{T}^{\leftarrow})|\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\leftarrow})]$ is a constant independent of $h_{t}$.
L248: The proof of Proposition cite144†3.4 can be found in Appendix cite33†B . Since the expectation in the population risk (cite143†3.16 ) is computationally intractable, we approximate it by empirical risk using independent and identically distributed samples:
L249: 
L250:  | $$\widehat{{\mathcal{J}}}_{t}(h_{t})\coloneq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|h_{t}(\mu_{T-t}\mathbf{X}_{0}^{i}+\sigma_{T-t}{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{i})-w(\mathbf{X}_{0}^{i})\|_{2}^{2},$$  |  | (3.17)
L251: where $\mathbf{X}_{0}^{1},\ldots,\mathbf{X}_{0}^{n}$ are independent and identically distributed random variables drawn from the base distribution $p_{0}$, and ${\bm{\varepsilon}}_{1},\ldots,{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{n}$ are independent standard Gaussian random variables. A naive approach for estimating the Doob’s $h$-function $h_{t}^{*}$ (cite141†3.10 ) involves vanilla empirical risk minimization:
L252: 
L253:  | $$\widehat{h}_{t}\in\argmin_{h_{t}\in{\mathscr{H}}_{t}}\widehat{{\mathcal{J}}}_{t}(h_{t}),$$  |  | (3.18)
L254: where ${\mathscr{H}}_{t}$ is a hypothesis class, which is chosen as a neural network class in this work.
L255: #### Limitations of vanilla regression
L256: 
L257: It is crucial that estimating the Doob’s guidance $\nabla\log h_{t}^{*}$ in (cite139†3.14 ) necessitates not only the estimation of the Doob’s $h$-function $h_{t}^{*}$ but also its gradient $\nabla h_{t}^{*}$, as expressed by
L258: 
L259:  | $$\nabla\log h_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{z})=\frac{\nabla h_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{z})}{h_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{z})},\quad\mathbf{z}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}.$$  |
L260: Previous research, including classifier guidance (cite58†Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ), Monte Carlo regression cite64†Uehara et al. (2025b, Section 2.2) and cite127†Ouyang et al. (2024) , approaches this challenge by approximating the Doob’s $h$-function $h_{t}^{*}$ with the vanilla empirical risk minimizer $\widehat{h}_{t}$ (cite145†3.18 ), and subsequently approximating the gradient of the Doob’s $h$-function $\nabla h_{t}^{*}$ via the plug-in gradient estimator $\nabla\widehat{h}_{t}$.
L261: Although rigorous theoretical studies (cite103†Bauer and Kohler, 2019 ; cite146†Nakada and Imaizumi, 2020 ; cite104†Schmidt-Hieber, 2020 ; cite105†Kohler and Langer, 2021 ; cite147†Farrell et al., 2021 ; cite148†Kohler et al., 2022 ; cite106†Jiao et al., 2023 ) demonstrate that the vanilla empirical risk minimizer $\widehat{h}_{t}$ converges to the Doob’s $h$-function $h_{t}^{*}$ in the $L^{2}$-norm, the convergence of the corresponding plug-in gradient estimator $\nabla\widehat{h}_{t}$ cannot be guaranteed, which has been mentioned in cite90†Mou (2025, Section 3.2.2) .
L262: To illustrate this fundamental limitation, consider the sequence of functions $f_{n}:{\mathcal{I}}\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}$, defined as $x\mapsto n^{-1}\sin(nx)$, and the zero function $f_{0}:{\mathcal{I}}\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}$, where ${\mathcal{I}}:=[0,2\pi]$. While $\|f_{n}-f_{0}\|_{L^{p}({\mathcal{I}})}\rightarrow 0$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$, we observe that $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\|f_{n}^{\prime}-f_{0}^{\prime}\|_{L^{p}({\mathcal{I}})}\neq 0$ for each $1\leq p\leq\infty$.

L265: #### Doob’s matching with gradient penalty
L266: 
L267: To simultaneously estimate the Doob’s $h$-function and its gradient, we adopt gradient-penalized regression (cite149†Drucker and Le Cun, 1991 ; cite150†Drucker and Le Cun, 1992 ; cite151†Ding et al., 2025 ). L272: By a similar argument as (cite152†3.17 ), we can also introduce an empirical counterpart of (cite153†3.19 ):

L274:  | $$\widehat{{\mathcal{J}}}_{t}^{\lambda}(h_{t})\coloneq\widehat{{\mathcal{J}}}_{t}(h_{t})+\frac{\lambda}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|\nabla h_{t}(\mu_{T-t}\mathbf{X}_{0}^{i}+\sigma_{T-t}{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{i})\|_{2}^{2},$$  |  | (3.20)

Then we have a gradient penalized empirical risk minimizer:

L277:  | $$\widehat{h}_{t}^{\lambda}\in\argmin_{h_{t}\in{\mathscr{H}}_{t}}\widehat{{\mathcal{J}}}_{t}^{\lambda}(h_{t}),$$  |  | (3.21)
L278: where ${\mathscr{H}}_{t}$ is a hypothesis class, which is chosen as a neural network class in this work.
L279: ###### Remark 3.5.
L280: 
L281: In Section cite27†4.3 , we will demonstrate that not only does the gradient-penalized estimator $\widehat{h}_{t}^{\lambda}$ in (cite154†3.21 ) converges to the Doob’s $h$-function $h_{t}^{*}$, but its gradient $\nabla\widehat{h}_{t}^{\lambda}$ also approaches $h_{t}^{*}$, provided that the regularization parameter $\lambda$ and the hypothesis class ${\mathscr{H}}_{t}$ are chosen appropriately.
L282: #### Doob’s guidance estimation
L283: 
L284: The Doob’s matching with gradient penalty (cite154†3.21 ) yields a valid estimator of the Doob’s guidance:
L285: 
L286:  | $$\widehat{\mathbf{g}}_{t}^{\lambda}(\mathbf{z})\coloneq\nabla\log\widehat{h}_{t}^{\lambda}(\mathbf{z})=\frac{\nabla\widehat{h}_{t}^{\lambda}(\mathbf{z})}{\widehat{h}_{t}^{\lambda}(\mathbf{z})}\approx\frac{\nabla h_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{z})}{h_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{z})}=\nabla\log h_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{z}),\quad\mathbf{z}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}.$$  |  | (3.22)
L287: This plug-in Doob’s guidance estimator $\widehat{\mathbf{g}}_{t}^{\lambda}$ is characterized by the gradient-penalized regressor $\widehat{h}_{t}^{\lambda}$ in (cite154†3.21 ), thus termed the regressor-guidance.
L288: ### 3.4  A summary of procedure
L289: 
L290: By a similar argument as Section cite13†2.4 , we have the exponential integrator for the controllable diffusion model:
L291:  | $\displaystyle\,\mathrm{d}\widehat{\mathbf{Z}}_{t}^{\leftarrow}$  | $\displaystyle=(\widehat{\mathbf{Z}}_{t}^{\leftarrow}+2\widehat{\mathbf{s}}(kh,\widehat{\mathbf{Z}}_{kh}^{\leftarrow})+2\widehat{\mathbf{g}}^{\lambda}(kh,\widehat{\mathbf{Z}}_{kh}^{\leftarrow}))\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}_{t},\quad t\in(kh,(k+1)h),$  |  | (3.23)
L292:  | $\displaystyle\widehat{\mathbf{Z}}_{0}^{\leftarrow}$  | $\displaystyle\sim{\mathcal{N}}({\mathbf{0}},\mathbf{I}_{d}),$  |
L293: where $0\leq k\leq K-1$, the pre-trained base score estimator $\widehat{\mathbf{s}}$ is defined as (cite107†2.5 ), and the Doob’s guidance estimator $\widehat{\mathbf{g}}^{\lambda}$ is defined as (cite155†3.22 ).
L294: We apply post-processing to the generated particle $\widehat{\mathbf{Z}}_{T-T_{0}}^{\leftarrow}$ to ensure numerical stability and facilitate the theoretical analysis presented in Theorem cite92†4.5 (cite156†Lee et al., 2023a ; cite157†Chen et al., 2023 ). First, we assume the target distribution $q_{0}$ is concentrated on a domain centered at the origin, such as a distribution with compact support (Assumption cite158†1 ) or with light tails.

Second, because the controllable diffusion process is terminated at an early-stopping time $T_{0}$, there exists a mean shift between the target distribution $q_{0}$ and the early-stopping distribution $q_{T_{0}}\approx\widehat{q}_{T-T_{0}}$, as indicated by (cite160†2.2 ). To mitigate this drift, we employ a scaling operator.

L328: ## 4  Convergence Analysis
L329: 
L330: In this section, we establish a non-asymptotic convergence rate analysis for Doob’s matching (cite154†3.21 ) and the induced controllable diffusion model (cite159†3.23 ) introduced in Section cite14†3 .
L331: 
L332: ### 4.1  Assumptions
L333: 
L334: We begin by outlining the essential technical assumptions required for our theoretical results.
L335: ###### Assumption 1 (Bounded support).
L336: 
L337: The support of the target distribution $q_{0}$ is a compact set contained within the hypercube $\{\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}:\|\mathbf{x}\|_{\infty}\leq 1\}$.
L338: Assumption cite158†1 is a standard condition imposed on the data distribution (cite156†Lee et al., 2023a ; cite100†Oko et al., 2023 ; cite162†Chang et al., 2025a ; cite163†Beyler and Bach, 2025 ). This constraint is well-motivated by practical applications; for instance, image and video data consist of bounded pixel values, thereby satisfying this requirement.
L339: ###### Assumption 2 (Bounded weight function).
L340: 
L341: The weight function $w$ defined in (cite131†3.1 ) is bounded from above and bounded away from zero. Specifically, there exist constants $0<\underline{B}<1<\overline{B}<\infty$ such that
L342: 
L343:  | $$\underline{B}\leq w(\mathbf{x})\leq\bar{B},\quad\text{for all}\penalty\ \mathbf{x}\in\mathrm{supp}(q_{0}).$$  |
L344: Assumption cite164†2 implies that the base distribution $p_{0}$ and the tilted distribution $q_{0}$ satisfy mutual absolute continuity, ensuring that their supports coincide (i.e., $\mathrm{supp}(p_{0})=\mathrm{supp}(q_{0})$). This condition is crucial for establishing the regularity of Doob’s $h$-function.
L345: Furthermore, the ratio $\kappa\coloneq\bar{B}/\underline{B}$ serves as a condition number that characterizes the difficulty of the controllable diffusion task, as discussed in the context of posterior sampling by cite60†Purohit et al. (2025) ; cite56†Ding et al. (2024b) ; cite52†Chang et al. (2025b) .
L346: ###### Assumption 3 (Base score estimation error).
L347: 
L348: The base score estimator $\widehat{\mathbf{s}}$ defined in (cite107†2.5 ) satisfies the following error bound:
L349: 
L350:  | $$\frac{1}{T}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}h{\mathbb{E}}^{{\mathbb{P}}}\left[\|\widehat{\mathbf{s}}(kh,\mathbf{X}_{kh}^{\leftarrow})-\nabla\log p_{T-kh}(\mathbf{X}_{kh}^{\leftarrow})\|_{2}^{2}\right]\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{base}}^{2}.$$  |
L351: Assumption cite165†3 requires the $L^{2}$-error of the base score estimator $\widehat{\mathbf{s}}$ to be bounded with respect to the base path measure ${\mathbb{P}}$. In our setting, where numerous samples from the base distribution $p_{0}$ are available, estimators satisfying this bound can be obtained via implicit score matching (cite96†Hyvärinen, 2005 ), sliced score matching (cite97†Song et al., 2020 ), or denoising score matching (cite98†Vincent, 2011 ).
